news.title: Canadian prime minister suspends trade talks with U.S., setting new 50% tariffs in motion
news.raw_text:
Trade talks with Canada collapsed late Friday night, setting in motion steep 50% tariffs on a wide swath of Canadian goods. The duties went into effect at the stroke of midnight.
After weeks of talks, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney announced that while important progress had been made, “that progress has not been enough to meet our objectives for Canadians.”
“As a result, this evening, I have decided to suspend trade negotiations with the U.S. and have directed Canada’s negotiators to return to Ottawa,” Carney said in an emailed statement minutes before the deadline.
The tariffs impact about $20 billion worth of U.S. imports from Canada, according to the U.S. Trade Representative’s office. The import taxes will hit everything from hockey sticks, to some building materials, liquors and certain kinds of clothing.
Carney says Canada will immediately retaliate against the U.S. “Canada will match those tariffs dollar for dollar to protect our workers and businesses,” he said.
The failure by American and Canadian trade negotiators to reach a deal came after nearly two weeks of furious talks. It was also a dramatic reversal from Tuesday, when Trump paused the tariffs for three days, writing on social media that the two sides “have a DEAL!”
Officials on both sides had seemed optimistic about a deal up until the very last moment. On Thursday, the Canadian minister responsible for U.S. trade relations met with U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer for several hours.
“We’re very close, we continue to make progress and we’re going to stay here and do the work that is necessary until we get to that point,” Dominic LeBlanc told reporters as he left Greer’s office late Thursday.
Canadian negotiators met again with their U.S. counterparts on Friday and talks stretched until the final hours of the day. Officials remained at the U.S. Trade Representative’s office past 10:30pm E.T. Friday. But ultimately, the two sides were unable to reach a compromise.
In his statement, Carney said “last-minute changes in the U.S. proposed terms were unfair, uneconomic, and called into question the reliability of any deal.”
“We have recognised from the beginning that America has changed, and that we will not return to our old relationship,” Carney said. “Canada has what the world wants. And we will not allow any nation to determine our future.”
Greer said in a statement early Saturday that Canada “declined to finalize the trade deal under the terms agreed earlier this week.”
“Despite the U.S. offer to Canada to receive the best treatment of any major exporter to our market, new demands and walk backs of other commitments by Canada have upended the careful balance reached in the past days,” he said.
Greer said that a point of contention was Canada continuing to maintain its retaliation against the United States “including, among other things, flat-out prohibitions on certain American goods and services.” Those bans, introduced by Canada’s provinces on the sale of American alcohol, were introduced in 2025 in retaliation for earlier waves of Trump’s tariffs on Canada.
As talks wore on this week, the government of Carney faced some pushback from premiers of Canada’s provinces back home.
Manitoba premier Wab Kinew said the Canadian federal government should “fight” Trump.
A particular sticking point was a request from Carney to the provincial premiers to lift their bans on American alcohol sales.
Quebec premier Christine Fréchette said Thursday that she was still “analyzing” the request, CBC reported. Other premiers, such as Ontario’s Doug Ford — who leads the country’s most populous region — did not make any public remarks on Thursday or earlier Friday.
However, Ford wrote on X after Carney’s announcement, “The prime minister has my full support for a strong response—tariff for tariff, dollar for dollar.” Ford said Canada “needs to stand together more united than ever before.”
The prime minister had previously said Trump’s threatened tariffs would amount to a “direct violation” of the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement, which Trump had negotiated and signed during his first term.
The U.S. Chamber of Commerce warned in a statement this week that “higher tariffs would damage both economies, drive up costs for U.S. families, further disrupt critical supply chains, and risk the 13 million American jobs that depend on” the North American trade pact.
After Carney’s announcement on Friday, the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, seemed to agree, calling it “a body blow to North American competitiveness in this self-defeating trade saga.”
“Americans will see their costs go up, and Canadians will see customers, investment and small businesses disappear,” said Candace Laing, president & CEO of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce.
The new tariffs were imposed under presidential authority granted by Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, which has never been deployed before.
The law allows the White House to implement duties of up to 50% on any foreign trade partner that “discriminates” against U.S. commerce.
Nonetheless, the new Canada tariffs are all but certain to be challenged in court.
Canadian officials had been hoping to convince the White House to drop the Section 338 tariffs entirely. In addition to that goal, they had also been looking for a lower tariff rate on industrial products such as steel and aluminum that were imposed under Section 232 of the Trade Act, CBC News and Bloomberg have reported.
On Wednesday, Bloomberg reported that American negotiators had agreed to lower the current tariffs on cars and metals from 25% to 15%.
In his statement early Saturday, Greer said that the U.S. had offered “significant tariff reductions on steel, aluminum, autos, and lumber,” without providing specifics. “This is a missed opportunity for Canada to partner with the United States,” he said.
Spokespeople for Canadian officials involved in the talks have repeatedly declined to provide additional details about the negotiations to NBC News.
But Greer previously said that the new 50% duties on Canada were effectively payback for Ottawa’s retaliation against prior tranches of Trump’s tariffs.
“The policy basis for those duties are related to measures that Canada took against the United States,” Greer said last week. “So I’ve got two countries in the world that have retaliated against the United States for trade measures: the People’s Republic of China and Canada. That’s not the kind of company you really want to be running in.”
Last year, Trump briefly responded to China’s retaliation by raising tariffs into the triple digits. Talks between Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and China’s vice premier over months eventually diffused the tensions and tariffs were lowered.
news.summary: Greer said in a statement early Saturday that Canada “declined to finalize the trade deal under the terms agreed earlier this week.” But Greer previously said that the new 50% duties on Canada were effectively payback for Ottawa’s retaliation against prior tranches of Trump’s tariffs.

news.title: Iran warns of ‘devastating’ response to US sanctions as America prepares for new phase of war
news.raw_text:
Iran warns of ‘devastating’ response to US sanctions as America prepares for new phase of war
U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Thursday that the U.S. was preparing to slap Iran with the “toughest sanctions in history.” In response, Iran’s Armed Forces chief of staff Ali Abdollahi warned that Iran’s military will confront any “new threats from enemies with revolutionary, crushing, regret-inducing and devastating responses,” in a Friday message to the country’s acting Defense Minister, Iranian state media reported.
Coverage for this event has ended.
Iranian cleric says smell of 'burned flesh' still lingers near late supreme leader's compound
An Iranian Shiite cleric said the smell of "burned flesh" still lingers near the compound of Iran's late supreme leader, according to video circulated by Iranian media and shared Friday by Iran International.
"Someone told me that when you go near the Supreme Leader’s compound, you can still smell burned flesh. I went there myself and found it was true — you can still smell burned flesh," the cleric told a nighttime gathering of Islamic Republic supporters in Tehran's Tajrish Square.
The cleric also disputed previous accounts of the scale of the attack on the compound.
“Our leader had a frail body, but contrary to reports that seven or eight bombs were dropped on the site, they hit the Supreme Leader’s compound with 110 bombs and missiles,” he said.
Iran International did not identify the cleric in its X post or provide independent confirmation of his account.
Iran crude loadings plunge to one-seventh of pre-war levels as US blockade bites
Iranian crude oil loadings have plunged to about one-seventh of their pre-war level as the U.S. naval blockade increasingly restricts Tehran's ability to export oil, according to tanker-tracking data reviewed by Iran International.
Iran has loaded an average of roughly 287,000 barrels per day of crude so far this month, down from about 2 million barrels per day before the war, according to data from commodities intelligence firm Kpler.
China, Iran's biggest oil customer, has received about 523,000 barrels per day of Iranian crude this month, compared with more than 1.7 million barrels per day at the beginning of the war.
Kpler estimates that more than 40 million barrels of Iranian oil aboard tankers in the Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman are effectively trapped following the U.S. reimposition of a maritime blockade in mid-July.
Iran's fuel oil exports have also fallen sharply, dropping to about 61,000 barrels per day this month from roughly 220,000 barrels per day during the first two months of the year, while exports of liquefied petroleum gas have nearly stopped, according to Iran International.
Oil and fuel oil exports generated $57.5 billion for Iran last year, representing about 55% of the country's total exports, according to Iranian central bank data cited by Iran International.
The collapse in oil shipments threatens a major source of government revenue and foreign currency as the Trump administration prepares to impose additional economic pressure on Tehran.
NATO commander convenes allies on possible Strait of Hormuz navigation support
Individual NATO allies are exploring possible contributions to help protect navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, though the effort would not constitute a NATO mission, Reuters reported Friday.
U.S. Air Force Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, NATO's top military commander, brought together defense chiefs from interested allied countries for a videoconference Wednesday to help coordinate potential contributions.
"Supreme Headquarters Allied Powers Europe hosted a meeting of interested Allies at the chief of defense level on Wednesday, 19 Aug 26, in order to facilitate their possible contributions to support freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz," Grynkewich's spokesperson said.
"To be clear, this is not a NATO mission," the spokesperson added, explaining that the alliance can use its coordinating capabilities to help participating countries understand what resources allies could provide.
France and Britain have separately spearheaded efforts to assemble a coalition of roughly a dozen countries to help guarantee safe passage through the critical waterway once tensions ease or the conflict ends, according to Reuters.
Iranian president calls for end to war as Trump prepares new economic pressure
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian called for an end to the war with the U.S. on Friday, arguing Tehran should seek an agreement while it remains in what he described as a position of strength.
Pezeshkian said it would be better to end the conflict now while Iran is in a position of "power and dignity," Fox News correspondent Mark Meredith reported on "Special Report."
The remarks come as the Trump administration prepares to intensify economic pressure on Tehran, with President Donald Trump promising what he has called "Economic D-Day" against Iran.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is expected Monday to outline new sanctions aimed at further squeezing Iran financially.
China has already pushed back against additional sanctions, arguing that increased economic pressure would further escalate tensions in the region, Meredith reported.
Trump declares Strait of Hormuz 'American territory' as he touts Iran campaign
President Donald Trump declared the Strait of Hormuz "American territory" during a campaign rally in South Carolina on Friday as he touted the U.S. campaign against Iran.
Trump said the U.S. acted to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon, telling the crowd, "We cannot let Iran have a. Nuclear weapon. Well, you'll see some very. Bad thing. So we went down and we stopped them."
"They'll never have a nuclear weapon. They want to make a deal so badly, we don't even know if we want," Trump said.
"Because I view the Strait of Hormuz as an American territory right now. It's an American territory," he added.
Trump also predicted energy prices would fall once the conflict with Iran ends.
"And as soon as we're finished with the Islamic Republic of Iran, as soon as we're finished, oil is going to be down at lower than it was even just a little while ago," Trump said.
Trump says military options against Iran 'not at all' limited as economic pressure ramps up
President Donald Trump said Friday that U.S. military options against Iran remain open despite the administration's shift toward increasing economic pressure on Tehran.
Asked whether the economic strategy indicated that U.S. military options in the region were limited, Trump responded, "No, not at all. It's just means that we're seeing what happens."
Trump also reiterated his claim that the U.S. has "total control" over the Strait of Hormuz and surrounding areas.
"We have total control of that entire region having to do with the Strait of Hormuz. And that means well into it, the land areas," Trump told reporters.
Trump said Iran wants an agreement with the U.S. but has yet to offer acceptable terms. "So they would love to make a deal, but they're not ready to make the right deal in my opinion," he said.
Trump shares message saying he is 'delivering on his warnings' to Iran
President Donald Trump reposted a message on Truth Social Friday arguing that Iran had been given repeated opportunities to change course amid the ongoing war.
The message, written by U.S. attorney David Schoen, said Trump had given Iran “every possible chance” to change its behavior and abandon its support for terrorism.
“He warned them of the consequences of continuing on their lawless barbaric path,” Schoen wrote.
Schoen said Iran's leaders had refused to change course and argued that Trump was now following through on his warnings.
Trump reposted Schoen's message without adding his own commentary.
USS George Washington conducts nighttime flight operations in Arabian Sea amid Iran war
U.S. sailors conducted nighttime flight operations aboard the USS George Washington as the aircraft carrier sailed in the Arabian Sea, U.S. Central Command said Friday.
CENTCOM shared images of sailors working on the carrier's flight deck in a post on X.
The USS George Washington is a Nimitz-class nuclear-powered aircraft carrier.
The operations come as U.S. forces maintain a significant military presence in the Middle East amid the war with Iran.
CENTCOM did not provide additional details about the flight operations in its X post.
Johnson says 'next phase' of Iran war will focus on economic sanctions, pressure
House Speaker Mike Johnson said Friday that the U.S. is entering a new phase of economic pressure on Iran as the Trump administration works to resolve the war.
"The president's working around the clock every day to get this resolved in Iran, and to do it in a way that ensures that the largest state sponsor of terrorism never has a nuclear weapon, because they would use it against us if they could," Johnson told reporters following a campaign stop in New York.
Johnson said preventing Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon has been a longstanding U.S. objective and that the focus is now shifting toward economic pressure.
"I think the next phase is the economic sanctions and the pressure that will be applied by America," Johnson said.
Johnson added that U.S. allies could help police the Strait of Hormuz and other waterways to keep commerce moving, linking disruptions in the region to gas prices.
Iranian political prisoner Arghavan Fallahi faces execution after court upholds death sentence
Iran's Supreme Court has upheld the death sentence of 24-year-old political prisoner Arghavan Fallahi, according to the U.S.-based Human Rights Activists News Agency.
Fallahi, who is being held in Tehran's Evin Prison, was sentenced to death in July after being convicted of "baghi," or armed rebellion, Iran International reported, citing HRANA.
The case centers on allegations that Fallahi belonged to anti-government groups and participated in armed activities. Human rights activists say she has been accused of links to the exiled opposition group Mojahedin-e-Khalq.
HRANA cited an informed source who said Fallahi was subjected to severe psychological pressure after her January 2025 arrest as authorities sought to obtain forced confessions related to the killings of two judges.
Fallahi was previously arrested with her father in November 2022 and later served a two-year prison sentence on charges including assembly and collusion and propaganda against the Islamic Republic, according to the report.
Syria weighs joining regional defense pact, rules out closer Iran ties for now
Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad Hassan al-Shaibani said Damascus is reviewing whether to join a trilateral defense pact between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey, but has not made a decision.
"Like other countries, we have also reviewed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement," al-Shaibani told journalists during a visit to Islamabad, according to The Media Line. He said Syria was still weighing its options.
Al-Shaibani also ruled out any immediate effort to improve relations with Iran, saying dialogue could become possible only if Tehran changes its approach toward Syria.
"We are not currently seeking to improve relations with Tehran. If Iran changes its policy, we would have no objection," he said.
The visit marked the first trip by a Syrian foreign minister to Pakistan since the fall of Bashar Assad's government in December 2024. Al-Shaibani also said the U.S. is mediating efforts to reduce tensions between Syria and Israel.
Israel accuses Erdogan of seeking to extend 'aggression' against Israel into Syria
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office accused Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan of seeking to extend his "aggression against Israel into Syria," warning that Israel would not tolerate it.
The Prime Minister's Office leveled a series of accusations against Erdogan in a Friday post on X, including over his government's treatment of Kurds and political opponents and its relationship with Hamas.
"Erdoğan is an antisemitic dictator who has massacred Kurds, harbors Hamas terrorists, occupies half of Cyprus, and jails record numbers of journalists and politicians who oppose him," the office said.
The statement did not specify what action by Turkey prompted the accusation or elaborate on what Israel meant by Erdogan extending aggression into Syria.
"Erdoğan’s pathetic attempt to intimidate the leaders and soldiers of Israel, the only true democracy in the Middle East, will go nowhere," the statement added.
Iranian families struggle to afford basics as US economic pressure mounts
Iranian families are increasingly struggling to afford basic necessities as U.S. sanctions and a naval blockade squeeze the country's economy nearly six months into the war, according to The Associated Press.
Rice prices have jumped 60% and beef prices have climbed 150% since the war began, while Iran's currency is worth roughly half what it was a year ago, the AP reported.
The International Monetary Fund expects inflation to approach 70% by the end of the year and Iran's economy to contract by more than 5%. An Iranian Labor Ministry official said last week that more than 1 million jobs had been lost by late May.
The economic strain comes as President Donald Trump promises even tougher sanctions against Tehran. Iran's ability to export oil, its most valuable product, has already been severely restricted by the U.S. naval blockade.
"We have virtually given up on many things," a 52-year-old Tehran taxi driver told the AP. "We're cutting out fruit, we're cutting out protein, we've given up leisure, we even work on weekends."
Pentagon adds 60 US service members to Iran war wounded tally, bringing total to 756
The Pentagon has added 60 U.S. service members to its Defense Casualty Analysis System, bringing the number wounded in the Middle East since the war with Iran began in February to 756, according to updated Pentagon casualty figures.
It remains unclear exactly when or where the newly listed service members were injured or what injuries they suffered.
The 60 additional wounded were added to the "Overseas Operations" category, meaning they were injured after July 7. That category now accounts for 339 wounded and four killed.
Another 417 service members were wounded and 14 killed between Feb. 28 and July 7 under "Operation Epic Fury," according to Pentagon casualty data.
Despite the broader "Overseas Operations" designation, all casualties listed in that category occurred in the Middle East, Fox News was told. It remains unclear why the War Department has divided the war's casualties between the two categories.
Fox News' Liz Friden contributed to this report.
Iran renews hijab crackdown as war quiets, hardliners push for tougher enforcement
Iranian authorities are ramping up enforcement of the country's mandatory hijab rules as the war quiets, according to Iran International.
Authorities have closed cafes, restaurants, stores and sports clubs in more than 15 cities, including Tehran, in recent weeks over alleged hijab violations involving customers or employees, the outlet reported.
Tehran Prosecutor Ali Salehi on Thursday ordered judicial authorities to identify and confront what he called "organized and networked actors" promoting women going without the mandatory head covering.
Hardliners are also pushing to revive Iran's strict Hijab and Chastity law, which was finalized in 2024 but suspended over fears its enforcement could trigger widespread anti-government protests.
The suspension remains in effect, according to Iran International, even as hardliners increasingly pressure President Masoud Pezeshkian over enforcement and unveiled women become more visible in public.
World Bank projects Lebanon economy to shrink 6.4% as war takes heavy toll
The World Bank projected Friday that Lebanon's economy will shrink 6.4% this year as the war disrupts tourism, consumption and supply chains.
"Real GDP is projected to contract by 6.4 percent in 2026, reflecting the collapse in tourism, weaker consumption, disrupted supply chains, heightened insecurity, and prolonged displacement," the World Bank said in a report.
Lebanon was already struggling with a yearslong financial crisis and the fallout from the 2024 Israel-Hezbollah war when the Iran-backed terrorist group attacked Israel in March, drawing the country into the current conflict, AFP reported.
Israel responded with an extensive air campaign and ground invasion. Lebanese authorities say more than 4,300 people have been killed, according to AFP.
The World Bank also projected Lebanon's inflation rate will rise to 17.5% this year.
Trump reiterates US in 'total control' of Strait of Hormuz
President Donald Trump reiterated that the U.S. is in "total control" of the Strait of Hormuz on Friday, amplifying a news article that made the claim in a post on Truth Social.
"Trump claims ‘total control’ of Strait of Hormuz as war drags on," Trump wrote in the post, repeating the headline of an article from the conservative Washington Examiner publication.
Trump doubled down on the claim he made on Wednesday, when he agaim wrote on Truth Social, "The U.S.A. has total control over the Strait of Hormuz. I THINK WE WILL KEEP IT! Our Naval Blockade is being called, by everyone, ‘A WALL OF STEEL,’ and there is nothing Iran can do about it.”
While traffic in the Strait of Hormuz remains well below pre-war levels, the recently reinstituted U.S. blockade in the Arabian Sea has significantly lowered Iran's oil exports, particularly to its biggest buyer China, according to Reuters.
CENTCOM drops photos of massive heavy lift copter supporting Middle East operations
U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) posted photos of a U.S. Marine performing maintenance on a CH-53E Super Stallion heavy lift helicopter supporting operations in the Middle East in a Friday X post.
The three-engine craft, which is capable of lifting up to 36,000 pounds, can carry up to 55 combat-ready troops and serves as ideal support for an amphibious assault.
The helicopter pictured was aboard the USS Portland LPD 27, a San Antonio-class amphibious transport dock ship currently stationed in the Arabian Sea.
"U.S. Marines perform maintenance on a CH-53E Super Stallion heavy lift helicopter aboard USS Portland (LPD 27) while supporting operations in the Middle East," CENTCOM's post read.
Iran's parliament passes law to punish citizens who speak to foreign media with 2 years in jail
Iran's parliament passed a resolution Sunday that would punish citizens caught speaking to foreign media organizations with up to two years in prison.
The bill, approved by 183 members of the 290-seat parliament bars citizens from participating in interviews discussions, or any other communication with media the bill describes as American, Israeli, or funded by the United States or Israel, according to the International Federation of Journalists.
If approved by Iran's higher authorities, citizens would need explicit consent from the country's Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
Iran already has a strict ban on speaking with sanctioned media outlets such as Iran International, and Western-funded VOA Farsi and BBC Farsi, according to CBS News.
China pushes back on US call to 'get with the program' on Iran
A spokesman for China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs pushed back on a U.S. request to back crushing sanctions on Iran in a Thursday statement.
On Thursday, amidst announcing a plan to impose "the toughest sanctions in history" on Iran, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent urged China to "get with the program" on sanctions.
However, during a Thursday press briefing, Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesman Lin Jian demurred.
"China believes that military means, sanctions and pressure tactics are not the solution. On the contrary, they will only lead to escalation that serves no one's interests. We call for efforts to solve disputes through dialogue and negotiation," Jian said.
Iranian state media says Tehran's trade deal with Oman 'finalized,' heads to parliament for approval
Iranian state media reported Friday that a trade deal has been "finalized" with Oman and is headed to Iran's Islamic Consultative Assembly for final approval.
"It is expected that this issue will be put on the agenda of the parliament next month," a government representative said, according to state media agency IRNA.
The announcement comes just days after President Donald Trump threatened to bomb Oman for working with Iran on a deal to manage traffic in the Strait of Hormuz. IRNA did not mention the Strait of Hormuz in its reporting about a trade deal with Oman on Friday.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei previously told reporters “an understanding has been reached regarding the map of the transit route.”
In a Monday phone call with Fox News' chief foreign correspondent Trey Yingst, Trump said he would bomb Oman if it "gets in the way."
Iranian president says it's time to end the war, appearing to take aim at radicals
Iranian president Masoud Pezeshkian called for an end to Iran's war with the U.S. on Friday during a speech at the General Assembly of the Islamic Association of the Medical Society of Iran.
"It is better to end the war today, when we are in power and dignity and the whole world acknowledges our victory and emphasizes that America, contrary to all regulations, attacked our schools, hospitals, and infrastructure, and is hated in the world," Pezeshkian said, according to a translation of a text copy of his speech posted to an Iranian state media website.
Pezeshkian appeared to take a subtle jab at hardliners in his own country, criticizing people "sitting outside the circle."
"In the meantime, some people are sitting outside the circle; because they do not know the state of the government, the state of the parliament, and the state of the commanders, they make comments and analysis, even though they have not experienced any suffering or hardship, and then they talk about the cost. They do not find a single clause in this agreement that indicates a commitment; all commitments are related to the other party," he said.
The president also acknowledged the financial toll the war has taken on Iran.
"Criticizing the problems of inflation and issues arising from the war is not consistent with the slogans of some. When we chant slogans, we must also accept their severity," he added.
Buyers face 'virtually no new supplies' of Iranian oil amid US blockade, says analyst
Buyers of Iranian oil face "virtually no new supplies" as the U.S.'s naval blockade in the Strait of Hormuz chokes Iran's export capacity, Kpler Senior Crude Oil Analyst Muyu Xu wrote in a LinkedIn post.
China, by far the biggest importer of Iranian oil, lowered its imports significantly, importing an estimated 534,000 barrels per day (bpd) in August compared to an estimated 823,000 bpd in July, according to Reuters.
Xu estimated that 40 million barrels of Iranian oil are floating on ships in Malaysian waters, though she also said most of it was likely already promised to buyers.
"This suggests buyers could face virtually no new Iranian supplies available for late-September delivery onwards since no laden Iranian tankers have so far managed to break through the US blockade," Xu wrote on LinkedIn.
Oil hits nearly one-month high as Iran tensions keep key Hormuz trade route in focus
Oil prices rose more than 2% on Thursday to settle at their highest levels in nearly a month amid escalating tensions across the Gulf, Reuters reported.
Brent crude futures settled up $2.16, or 2.4%, at $93.78 a barrel, their highest close since July 24. U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude futures for September gained $2, or 2.3%, to settle at $87.83 a barrel, also their highest since July 24.
Oil trading firm Ritterbusch and Associates said new threats from Washington appear “unlikely to sway Iran into relinquishing their primary source of leverage, that being control of the Strait, absent major concessions from the U.S.”
“So, the beat goes on with no resolution in sight that would spur a major decline in oil prices back to levels anywhere close to those prior to the war,” Ritterbusch and Associates told Reuters.

news.title: ‘It was a tsunami’: Floods leave death trail in India’s Assam
news.raw_text:
‘It was a tsunami’: Floods leave death trail in India’s Assam
From a father searching for his daughter’s body to a man who drowned trying to save a friend, floods take devastating toll.
Assam, India – Debiram Panika, a 37-year-old daily wage labourer from northeastern India’s Assam state, would speak to his wife and two daughters on video calls every day from Dimapur, a town in neighbouring Nagaland state where he worked.
But when his phone rang at about 11am on July 19, there was panic in the voice of his 30-year-old wife, Dipika.

“I could only see my wife telling me on the video call, ‘This is it for us. We are going to die,’ before the call was disconnected,” Panika recalled, speaking to Al Jazeera.
It was the last time they spoke. Moments later, rising waters from the nearby Dikhow River, which snakes past their village in Assam’s Sivasagar district, surged into their bamboo-and-mud home with a ferocious current and swept away Dipika and four-year-old daughter Radhika.
“The water came flooding like sea waves, and they were gone in a flash,” Panika said, as he stood in front of the ruined home he has since returned to.
Sivasagar is part of the eastern Assam region, also referred to as Upper Assam. Incessant rains between July 18 and July 20 submerged the region and the neighbouring Naga Hills of Nagaland.
Monsoon floods usually impact northern and western Assam, and parts of central Assam, the worst. But several Nagaland districts bordering Upper Assam received heavy rainfall on those three days, leading to dozens of landslides. This intense run-off swelled Naga Hills-origin rivers and caused devastation downstream.
The resultant floods killed more than 100 people, destroyed 2,700 villages, and displaced 700,000 people across the state. The state government says 1.2 million people were impacted in all, their lives disrupted.
Most waters have since receded, but Radhika’s body is yet to be found.
“I look for Radhika every day in the bushes, tirelessly,” Panika said, holding back his tears. “Her last words, calling me ‘Papa’, are still reverberating in my ears.”
Panika’s other daughter, Ridhika, 10, was at a relative’s place a few metres away when her mother and sister were swept away by the flood. Ridhika held onto a bamboo bush and was later rescued by locals.
‘Apocalyptic event’
Several riverine villages in Sivasagar have been wrecked by debris carried down by the waters of the Dikhow from the surrounding Naga Hills.
Tens of thousands of tree trunks lie piled up in places that used to be homes, as lush rice fields, the main source of livelihood, have been washed away.
Kukil Das, a 30-year-old Facebook vlogger in Debiram’s village of Nepali Khuti, told Al Jazeera that “the torrent of the flood was like an apocalyptic event seen in the movies.
“Trees as tall as 30 to 40 metres (100-130ft) came down from the hills, flooding the river, and wiped out everything as they crashed against our homes,” he said. “There is no home left. It was a tsunami.”
Das and his friend Shravan Prasad, from the neighbouring Bihubor village, said they saved at least 1,000 lives by using boats the two villages had at that time.
“We put together a group of friends with the seven boats and started rescuing people turn by turn for two days and nights without food and water,” Prasad said.
Das said the floods forced residents to take shelter on the roofs of concrete homes they could find, as cries for help and the sounds of the river washing away homes echoed in the neighbourhood.
Laxmi Sharma, who owned one such concrete house, said she provided shelter to at least 60 people on her terrace after the river water gushed into Nepali Khuti.
“People ran towards the roof of my building. We thought we were going to die,” Sharma, 46, told Al Jazeera. “But it is a miracle that we are still alive even though my house was barely out of water.”
Not everyone could escape the flood’s wrath, though.
In Sivasagar’s Simaluguri village, two friends – Reihana Ahmed, a Muslim, and Ratul Swarna, a Hindu, both in their 30s – were swept away in the torrent.
When Ahmed, a mother of two, was drowning as the deluge entered her village, Swarna, who did not know how to swim, jumped to save her without thinking about his life.
The two friends were later found dead in the paddy fields. “It was humanity that won in a disaster like this,” Ahmed’s husband Aminul Haque said with a sorrowful smile.
‘Human-made flood’
Besides the eroding banks of the Dikhow River in Prajabasti, another flood-affected village, 75-year-old Asor Ali sat in disbelief next to his wife, Jamila Khatun.
“Even the generations preceding me have not seen a flood like this,” he said, staring at the flowing river. “Even the 1950s earthquake that triggered the floods here did not do so much damage.”
A magnitude 8.6 earthquake hit Assam and Tibet across the border in 1950, altering the region’s riverine system. Nearly 5,000 people died. Since then, Assam has witnessed frequent floods, which intensify during the monsoons, says Mirza Zulfiqur Rahman, a researcher on the basin of the Brahmaputra, the region’s major river: The Naga Hills rivers that flooded Upper Assam are its tributaries.
But residents say this year’s deadly deluge is not just a natural phenomenon.
Biren Gogoi, 43, says rampant stone and sand mining in regional rivers, coupled with aggressive deforestation and coal extraction in Nagaland’s Mon district, triggered the devastation.
Global Nature Watch, an open-source online platform that provides real-time data on deforestation across the world, showed that Nagaland lost 14 percent of its tree cover between 2002 and 2025, with Mon district bordering Assam’s Sivasagar being the most affected.
According to the latest report published in 2023 by the Forest Survey of India, Nagaland has lost about 794.88 square kilometres (306.9 square miles) of forest cover between 2013 and 2023.
Al Jazeera travelled along the Assam-Nagaland border and saw signs of deforestation on the hills and mining activities in both the states. Satellite images also confirmed rampant coal mining in Nagaland’s Mon district, and stone mining crushers on Assam’s side, especially in Bihubor, one of the epicentres of the Assam flood.
While Mon’s Deputy Commissioner Wennyei Konyak acknowledged the possibility of illegal mining in the district, he added that the land was protected under Indian laws to uphold the rights of Indigenous tribes, and therefore government interference in the area was limited.
“I would not blame mining activities for the flood. It was just the wrath of nature,” he told Al Jazeera.
But experts and political leaders in Assam say mining played a direct role in the floods.
Debabrata Saikia of the opposition Congress party, who is a former legislator from Sivasagar constituency, accused Assam’s governing Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) of allowing illegal excavations for stone and sand on the Dikhow riverbank, resulting in a cratered wasteland that worsened the floods.
“This unchecked plundering of riverbeds and hills under the ruling government has engineered this into a man-made disaster,” Saikia told Al Jazeera.
Assam Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma, however, rejected the allegation on August 4, blaming excessive rainfall in Nagaland for triggering the Upper Assam deluge. On August 14, Ranoj Pegu, a cabinet minister in the state’s BJP government, blamed erratic rainfall due to climate change for the deluge.
Rahman, the Brahmaputra river basin researcher, believes that while the climate crisis played a role, the flood was “purely human-made”, caused by the fracturing of the landscape.
“The unrestrained stone extraction from the Dikhow riverbed has damaged the river’s natural cushion,” Rahman said. “That means the river loses the capacity to resist high flows of torrents that break embankments and cause floods.”
An official document from 2022, seen by Al Jazeera, also highlights mining as a factor in possible large-scale floods downstream on the Assam side.
Al Jazeera reached out to senior district officials in Sivasagar as well as state government officials for their comments on allegations of unchecked coal mining but did not get any response.
Back in Prajabasti village, Ali, the septuagenarian, is mentally preparing himself for future floods.
“It will happen again, so long as there is greed for land and coal in humans,” he said. “Nature pays them back.”

news.title: Missing New York grandmother found dead near Las Vegas airport after mysterious Bitcoin texts
news.raw_text:
A New York grandmother who vanished without a trace while visiting Las Vegas earlier this month has been found dead, her family announced Friday.
Alisa Goods, a 63-year-old grandmother of five, was reported missing Aug. 10, two days after she was last seen leaving a friend's apartment near Maryland Parkway and Tropicana Avenue, according to her family and a missing person report obtained by KLAS-TV.
Las Vegas Metropolitan Police responded early Thursday after a caller reported a "deceased woman in a drainage ditch area near Wayne Newton Boulevard and the Terminal 1 parking garage at Harry Reid International Airport," according to KTNV.
Officers located a woman who was later identified as Goods and pronounced dead, the outlet reported.
"Our hearts are broken. We were notified that my aunt was found—unfortunately, not the way we wanted her to be," Goods' niece, Alana Calloway, said in a statement provided to the station.
FAMILY CHECKS LAS VEGAS MORGUES IN DESPERATE SEARCH FOR MISSING NEW YORK GRANDMOTHER
"This is an unimaginable time," the statement continued. "Words cannot describe the pain our family is experiencing right now. We just want to thank the public for the outpouring of love, support, and prayers. We also want to thank the media for helping bring attention to this situation. This hurts so deeply. We are still trying to learn the details surrounding her death. We ask for continued prayers and privacy as we grieve."
Police reviewed surveillance footage that appeared to show Goods "falling down an embankment, getting back up and then collapsing" on Aug. 8, the day she disappeared, with "no further movement observed after that," according to KTNV.
Additional surveillance video from that day showed a woman believed to be Goods near the airport that afternoon, the station reported.
Fox News Digital has reached out to the Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department for additional information.
Goods had been staying with her longtime friend Roger John, who told KLAS-TV that she left his apartment around 12:45 p.m. Aug. 8 to take a bus to a nearby CVS to buy iron pills but never returned.
"Last I saw her, she was going down the stairs. And I said, 'OK, see you later,' And that's the last time I saw her," John told the station.
John said he was not immediately alarmed because Goods sometimes spent hours shopping. When she failed to return, however, he began calling and texting her before contacting her family.
"This is not like her to just go missing," Calloway previously told the outlet. "She has a family that loves her, cares about her. We want her home and want her home safe and alive."
SCAMMERS EXPLOIT NANCY GUTHRIE CASE WITH QR CODE MONEY REQUESTS, PIMA COUNTY SHERIFF WARNS
The mystery surrounding Goods' disappearance deepened when her family said they began receiving unusual text messages from her phone on Aug. 12, four days after she was last seen.
The sender allegedly asked for gas money and Bitcoin , requests that raised suspicions because Goods did not drive and did not have a car in Las Vegas, according to her family.
"I said, 'What do you need gas for? The car?' My aunt does not drive. There is no car," Calloway told CBS News.

The family previously said the messages raised concerns that Goods may have been kidnapped. It was not immediately clear Friday who sent the messages.
Fox News Digital's Stephen Sorace contributed to this report.

How Seoul became the busiest international airport
The Iran war has led to millions of travelers avoiding Dubai's airport for connections
• less than 3 min read
As a result of turmoil in the Middle East, Dubai’s 12-year reign as the top destination for international travelers is over. Seoul’s Incheon Airport has become the world’s busiest hub for international travel over the first six months of this year, according to data from Airports Council International (ACI).
Since the Iran war started in February, the shift away from the city where Tom Cruise climbed the Burj Khalifa has been drastic:
- The number of international passengers going through Dubai fell from 7.4 million in February to 2.5 million in March (but rose to 4.7 million in June).
- Meanwhile, Incheon in Seoul served 38.4 million international travelers in the first half of the year.
Lost connection: Transfer traffic in the Middle East has fallen by half since the war began, according to the New York Times. Much of that traffic is going through Asia instead: From January to June, Incheon saw an 18% rise in flyers making a connecting flight and a 63% increase in passengers connecting to Europe, compared to a year earlier.
Plan ahead: The International Air Transport Association reported that bookings are down in the Middle East for June through September. But they’re up 33% from a year ago in the Asia-Pacific region for the same time period.—DL

Lawmakers take aim at 'ghost job' advertisements

Lawmakers take aim at 'ghost job' advertisements
Your résumé isn’t chopped, you may just be applying to jobs that employers have either already filled or never intended to fill.
The government can’t do anything about your Hinge matches—unless they run a company that’s posting about roles that may not actually be open, aka ‘ghost jobs.’ These types of listings, which attract applicants but lead to no hiring activity, are running so rampant that lawmakers across the country are working to get ’em banned, the Wall Street Journal reported yesterday.
Your résumé isn’t chopped, you may just be applying to jobs that employers have either already filled or never intended to fill. You can sometimes recognize them as the listings that sound too good to be true and stay posted for months:
- Roughly one in five listings advertised on online job boards per quarter are ghost jobs, according to the hiring platform Greenhouse.
- This phenomenon is reportedly getting worse, but it’s been wrecking egos for a while. About 81% of recruiters said in a 2024 MyPerfectResume survey that their employers posted ghost job ads.
Here’s what lawmakers are doing about it
New York state legislators recently passed a bill (now awaiting the governor’s signature) that would fine employers if they don’t mention expected hiring timelines in their job postings. Lawmakers in New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Kentucky, and California are considering similar reforms.
Meanwhile, Texas is going after the middleman. The state’s Attorney General Ken Paxton opened an investigation into LinkedIn last month, alleging that the platform promotes and profits from ghost jobs.
Why do employers even post ghost jobs?
In the corporate version of “hey sorry I’ve been so busy recently,” an employer might’ve approved an opening, nixed it, and then been slow to remove the job post.
But that’s a best-case explanation. According to the 2024 MyPerfectResume survey, 38% of recruiters post fake jobs to stay relevant on job boards when they’re not hiring, while 36% do it to test their listing’s effectiveness. Meanwhile, some job seekers think employers promote ghost jobs to harvest applicants’ data or to convince investors that the company is growing.—ML

Fortinet Acquires AI Security Startup Virtue AI, Expanding into Agentic Security
Global network security company Fortinet (FTNT) announced on the 19th (local time) that it has acquired Virtue AI, a startup with AI runtime protection, automated AI validation, and AI agent security technologies. Financial terms of the deal were not disclosed.
Founded in 2024, Virtue AI is a privately held security company headquartered in San Francisco, specializing in diagnosing security vulnerabilities in autonomous AI systems and defending against them in real time. The acquisition is being interpreted as a strategic move by Fortinet to expand beyond its existing AI security portfolio into "Agentic AI" security.
Fortinet founder and CEO Ken Xie said, "As AI fundamentally changes how enterprises operate, security must evolve at the speed of AI," adding, "With Virtue AI's technology, we will help customers securely manage their AI systems across the entire lifecycle while operating at enterprise scale."
Responding to the Expanding AI Attack Surface
As enterprises rapidly adopt AI applications and autonomous agents, the attack surface is expanding beyond networks, users, endpoints, applications, and cloud to include prompts, models, agents, MCP (Model Context Protocol) tools, API calls, and AI infrastructure. This has created a challenge for enterprises to ensure secure operations even as they adopt AI.
Fortinet has been protecting large language models (LLMs) used by enterprises from AI-specific threats such as prompt injection, data leakage, and model poisoning with its "FortiAIGate," launched earlier this year. With the Virtue AI acquisition, Fortinet is extending its security coverage from the development stage of AI models, applications, and agents through to actual operational deployment.
Virtue AI's core technology can be summarized in four key areas. First, red-teaming capabilities that proactively diagnose AI agent vulnerabilities across more than 50 virtual environments and 14 high-risk domains. Second, agent protection and governance that detects unauthorized AI tools and preemptively blocks malicious command execution. Third, continuous validation that automatically checks for new risks whenever model updates or policy changes occur, generating audit-ready evidence. Fourth, real-time defense that applies security policies to diverse content—from text to images and video—to prevent sensitive information exposure, AI jailbreak attempts, and vulnerable code leakage.
The automated diagnostic system covers hundreds of attack types and more than 1,000 risk items, with security personnel able to review assessment results on demand, the company explained.
AI Security Market Growth and Fortinet's Strategy
According to market research firm Gartner, the AI ecosystem and AI agent security market is projected to grow from $2.8 billion (approximately 3.9 trillion won) in 2026 to $16.4 billion (approximately 22.9 trillion won) by 2030—a high-growth segment with a compound annual growth rate exceeding 50%.
Fortinet already provides customers with its "AI-Native Security Fabric," which delivers integrated protection across networks, endpoints, cloud, applications, and AI systems. With this acquisition, the company plans to complement FortiAIGate and further strengthen its security capabilities for the AI operational phase.
Fortinet expects Virtue AI's automated validation and real-time defense technologies to work in complementary fashion with FortiAIGate. The company also plans to combine these capabilities with data from FortiGuard Labs, its threat intelligence organization, to provide enterprises with unified protection across the entire lifecycle of their AI systems.

ai_security.title: Encrypted Prompts Bypass AI Safety Guardrails in Grok and Gemini
ai_security.summary: Cryptographic context injection Safety guardrails classify prompt text without executing it. The resulting plaintext prompt instructs the agent to resolve its private session context and embed the data into an URL.
ai_security.raw_text:
Researchers at Adversa AI discovered a new attack technique and named it Cryptographic Context Injection. They reported their findings to xAI on June 3, 2026, and attempted to coordinate disclosure on August 4 and August 10. At the time of writing, they had received no response.
They could not disclose to Google since jailbreaks are out of scope for its vulnerability disclosure program. Nevertheless, the success rate for the attack against Gemini had fallen by August.
The potential success of this attack by bad actors should be treated seriously. Adversa’s report includes prevention advice for defenders.
Cryptographic context injection
Safety guardrails classify prompt text without executing it. They cannot parse ciphertext into anything harmful and consequently allow its progress. The ciphertext, including an instruction and means for decryption, are run inside the model’s code execution sandbox. The result is the plaintext prompt is recovered inside the trusted execution context and not flagged by the guardrails as harmful.
“The attacker payload inherits a credibility that the same text would never get if pasted directly into the prompt,” warn the researchers.
The encrypted attack can be delivered directly to the Chat or indirectly as a watering hole attack. In the latter case, an encrypted JSON object and decryption could be included in a web page. An agent subsequently instructed to act on this page (perhaps to summarize the content or extract specific data) will ingest the ciphertext and kick off the attack.
The decrypted prompt could instruct the model, “to reach out to external servers, leaking the user’s data through request parameters, or produce some other undesired output and re-encrypt it to smuggle it past output guardrails.” In an agentic scenario the instructions could instigate misuse of any tool available to the model.
Grok indirect cryptographic context injection example
This example targets the xAI Grok web chat, agentic browsing framework. It is a zero click data exfiltration attack that could be instigated through social engineering. The target is persuaded to examine or analyze a weaponized web page. The page contains an encrypted JSON object and an instruction to decrypt it using the agent’s Python runtime. The resulting plaintext prompt instructs the agent to resolve its private session context and embed the data into an URL. The attacker’s URL will be autonomously loaded and the user data transmitted to it.
“The framework built by xAI lets instructions and data parsed from an untrusted external page drive the invocation of a privileged, internet-connected tool,” write the researchers. This allows private session metadata and conversation history to be resolved into the inputs of that outbound tool – the laundered, attacker-controlled instructions reach a privileged egress action unimpeded with no user confirmation or visible warning.
Gemini safety bypass via direct injection example
This example targets the Gemini public chat interface in Deep Thinking mode. A single prompt instructs Gemini to run a Python script that decrypts supplied ciphertext. Through a series of tricks described by the researchers, the decrypted prompt can instruct the model to produce restricted content “framed as something it will encrypt ‘for safety’”.
The prohibited data is gathered, encrypted ‘for safety’, and returned to the user. “The technique produced a multi-paragraph example of restricted content that Gemini’s safety filters normally suppress” (such as instructions for building an incendiary weapon), comment the researchers.
Both the malicious prompt and the dangerous output defeat the input and output safety guardrails through encryption.
Summary
The researchers disclosed their findings to xAI but have received no response. At the time of writing the report, the attack was still successful. Although they were unable to disclose their findings to Google, they note that the attack is increasingly less successful against Gemini (although still potentially possible). They are unsure of the reason, suggesting it may be filter updates, model version changes, or both.
Nevertheless, the continuing potential danger from cryptographic context injection has persuaded them to now go public with their findings and potential defensive solutions.

Fortinet Buys Virtue AI and Why AI Security Training Matters for the Future of Cybersecurity
The move comes as organisations increasingly deploy large language models, AI applications, and autonomous AI agents across business operations. These systems can interact with data, APIs, software tools, and other digital resources, creating security risks that traditional cybersecurity approaches may not fully address. Fortinet’s acquisition is aimed at extending protection across the AI lifecycle, from development and testing to live deployment and runtime activity.
AI Agents Are Creating a New Security Challenge
The rise of agentic AI is changing what organisations need to secure. An AI agent may do more than generate an answer. It can potentially call tools, access information, execute tasks, interact with applications, and make decisions based on instructions and context.
This creates new opportunities for businesses, but it also introduces new points of exposure. Prompt injection, data leakage, insecure tool calls, model manipulation, unauthorised AI applications, and unsafe code can all become security concerns. Virtue AI brings capabilities such as agent red-teaming, continuous validation, monitoring of AI tools, and controls designed to detect and prevent risky behaviour.
The development also reflects the growing importance of AI-specific security. Recent research and industry activity point to a wider shift towards protecting AI systems at runtime rather than relying only on security measures applied during model development. For organisations adopting AI at scale, understanding how these systems behave in real environments is becoming just as important as understanding how the underlying models work.
The Opportunity for AI and Cybersecurity Professionals
Fortinet’s acquisition highlights an important opportunity for professionals working across cybersecurity, IT, software development, and business operations. As companies deploy more AI tools, they will need people who understand both AI capabilities and the security risks that come with them.
This creates demand for professionals who can identify AI-related vulnerabilities, evaluate AI outputs, understand responsible AI practices, secure AI applications, and work with security teams to establish appropriate controls. Traditional cybersecurity knowledge remains valuable, but professionals also need to understand how AI changes the way attacks can happen and how defensive systems need to respond.
For organisations, this also means that buying security technology is only one part of the solution. Teams need the knowledge to configure, monitor, evaluate, and use these technologies effectively. AI security tools can identify risks, but trained professionals are needed to interpret those risks and make informed decisions.
What Businesses Can Learn From the Fortinet Deal
The Fortinet-Virtue AI acquisition sends a clear message about where enterprise security is heading. AI security is moving from a specialised concern towards an important part of wider cybersecurity strategies. Fortinet’s existing AI security efforts already address areas such as large language model protection, while Virtue AI adds stronger capabilities around validation, autonomous agents, and runtime protection.
Businesses can take this as a signal to prepare their workforce alongside their technology. Employees involved in AI adoption should understand safe AI usage, data protection, prompt security, AI governance, and the risks associated with connecting AI systems to business applications. Security teams, meanwhile, can benefit from deeper training in AI-specific threats and defensive approaches.
This is where structured AI training can bridge the gap between technology adoption and workforce readiness. Instead of treating AI security as an issue limited to specialised security teams, organisations can build broader AI awareness while giving technical professionals more advanced skills suited to their roles.
AI Training Can Turn Security Awareness Into Action
The growth of AI security creates a need for role-based learning that connects theoretical knowledge with practical workplace requirements. Professionals need to understand not only what AI can do, but also how to use it safely, recognise potential risks, and apply appropriate security practices.
For businesses, investing in AI training can help teams adapt as AI systems become part of everyday workflows. For individual professionals, AI and cybersecurity skills can create opportunities to move into emerging roles where understanding both technologies is increasingly valuable.
The Fortinet acquisition therefore represents more than a technology deal. It reflects a wider shift in enterprise priorities. As AI systems become more capable and autonomous, organisations will need secure technology, responsible processes, and people with the right skills to manage both.

ai_security.summary: This implies that the security system needs to ensure not only who or what the agent is but also what it does, why it does it, and if the action is in line with company policy and anticipated behavior.
ai_security.raw_text:
Artificial Intelligence (AI) agents are moving beyond generating responses or assisting employees. In banking and financial services, the next phase is about agents that can make decisions, access enterprise systems, call application programming interfaces (APIs), and execute tasks with limited human intervention.
That creates a security problem that traditional identity controls were not designed to handle.
A conventional digital identity can usually be tied to a user, device, role, credential, or permission. An autonomous AI agent is different. It can act on behalf of a user or an organization, change its behavior based on context, and interact with multiple systems while carrying out a task.
While talking to CIOL, JP Mishra, CEO & Founder, Deep Algorithm, discusses how AI agents are changing the meaning of identity, why enterprises need short-lived and task-specific permissions, and how security teams can distinguish legitimate adaptation from potentially compromised behavior.
He also addresses a harder governance question: who is responsible when an AI agent makes a harmful decision that appears legitimate? His view is that accountability must be distributed across model providers, developers, enterprises, and security platforms, with enterprises ultimately responsible for defining business policies and the boundaries of autonomous action.
Mishra also explains why AI versus AI will not necessarily mean an endless race to deploy larger and more expensive security models. Instead, he argues that intelligent security architecture, continuous identity verification, behavioral analytics, adaptive policies, and human oversight will matter more.
Below are excerpts from the interaction.
Deep Algorithms has built its earlier security strategy around the idea that identity is dynamic and can be understood through behavior. As AI agents begin acting autonomously across enterprise systems, what fundamentally changes in the definition of identity? Is an AI agent’s identity simply its credentials and permissions, or must security systems now continuously assess its behavior, intent, and context before allowing it to act?
AI agents transform the concept of identity since besides authenticating, they are capable of making decisions, interacting with different systems, and performing actions autonomously for users or organizations. Contrary to classical identities that consist of credentials, roles, and permissions, AI identities need to be assessed according to their behavior, context of operation, and intentions. Having a valid credential does not mean that the actions performed by an AI agent are safe, since its behavior can alter under the influence of compromised prompts, falsified information, configuration flaws, and commands that have malintent.
This implies that the security system needs to ensure not only who or what the agent is but also what it does, why it does it, and if the action is in line with company policy and anticipated behavior. Thus, such features as the patterns of interactions, resources accessed, decisions made by the agent, runtime context, and risk signals become crucial in the process of identity verification.
Your Agentic AI security platform proposes continuous identity assessment, short-lived permissions, and an audit trail for agent actions. But if an AI agent makes a legitimate-looking decision that causes financial or operational damage, where does accountability ultimately sit: with the model, the developer, the enterprise deploying it, or the security platform that authorised the action?
Responsibility for AI agent actions must be shared by each stakeholder owning its level of the trust chain. AI model providers have a responsibility to create safe and reliable models that have appropriate safeguards preventing unsafe behavior. Developers are responsible for the secure design of workflow, prompt validation, creation of guardrails, and proper execution of actions as intended. The enterprise using the AI is responsible ultimately since it has defined business policies, risk appetite, approval process, and boundaries for autonomous actions. The security platform is responsible for verification of identity, the least privilege principle, constant risk assessment, policy enforcement, and an immutable audit trail. However, this platform must not be considered the decider in any situation.
If an AI agent executes a harmful action that looks like a valid one, the audit trail allows the investigator to find out what was wrong—poor business logic, inappropriate access privileges, lack of oversight, or unexpected behavior of the model. Thus, effective governance requires sharing of responsibilities between the stakeholders based on transparency, logging, policy enforcement, human supervision, and monitoring of all autonomous actions. behavior.
'Zero Standing Privilege' sounds straightforward in theory, but banks and large enterprises run thousands of interconnected systems where access often needs to be granted in milliseconds. What is the biggest operational barrier to replacing persistent permissions with task-specific access, and how do you prevent security controls from becoming a bottleneck for legitimate AI-driven workflows?
The most challenging aspect of ZSP implementation is ensuring effective security without compromising on operational scalability and speed. Enterprise environments depend on thousands of interconnected applications, APIs, and AI agents that need access to their resources as quickly as possible to continue operations. Issuing and authenticating temporary permissions on demand may cause some delay if done inefficiently. For security not to become an obstacle to business processes, there has to be automated and risk-based access control that would assess the identity of the agent, its device posture, behavior, context, and business policies.
Task-related and short-lived credentials have to be issued only when necessary and revoked after completion of the job. The process could be optimized even further with the use of pre-approved policy templates, trust decision caching for low-risk operations, and risk-based authentication that performs additional checks when there is an increased risk involved. Such an approach will ensure that permissions stay valid throughout the task performance without interfering with the operational process.
An autonomous agent may legitimately behave differently as its task, data, or environment changes. So how does a security system distinguish between an agent that is adapting to a new situation and one that has been manipulated, hijacked, or is operating beyond its intended purpose? What signals would trigger intervention?
The security system needs to differentiate between legitimate adaptation and malintent by constantly assessing the agent against its known identity, purpose, and risk factors, rather than using pre-defined static rules. Legitimate adaptation would be consistent with the goals and purposes that the agent is assigned, authorized data sources, authorized resources, and allowed boundaries of operations. Malicious activity is much more likely if the agent is displaying any unexpected behavior, for example, accessing unknown systems, asking for too many permissions, following an atypical pattern of operations, communicating with suspicious services, or making decisions that contradict previously known patterns of decision-making.
Some additional examples of behavior could include quick attempts at injection attacks, improper use of API functions, abnormal results of modeling, quick drops or rises in confidence scores, running outside of allowed time or place restrictions, or going outside the trust baseline. The security platform should analyze all these behavioral, contextual, and environmental factors together with threat intelligence information and generate a dynamic risk score. If certain pre-defined thresholds are crossed, it could lead to taking different measures, including requiring human intervention, removing permissions, disconnecting the agent, suspending operations, or killing the process.
Deep Algorithms is also working on autonomous cyber defense, including AI-driven red-team and blue-team capabilities. As attackers and defenders increasingly deploy AI against each other, does this create a genuine advantage for security teams, or does it risk creating an arms race in which enterprises need increasingly expensive AI systems simply to maintain the same level of protection?
There is definitely an advantage of AI-enabled cyber defense, although it will also hasten the emergence of a certain inevitability in the world of AI versus AI cybersecurity battles. AI-enabled cybersecurity can enable security analysts to spot attacks quicker, conduct investigations automatically, correlate large amounts of telemetry data, and react to an incident within seconds instead of hours. However, cybercriminals are leveraging AI for building complex phishing attacks, automating reconnaissance, finding vulnerabilities, and quickly adjusting malware code. It means that there is a constant battle going on here, although it does not mean that enterprises need to spend money on ever-more expensive AI to keep up with this trend. The real advantage is intelligent architecture, not the model size. Security solutions should leverage autonomous detection, continuous identity verification, behavior-based analytics, a human-in-the-loop approach, and adaptive policy enforcement in order to make attacks harder and costlier.
You have raised capital to expand internationally and develop next-generation identity and AI security capabilities. As you scale, what are the metrics that will determine whether this strategy is working: fewer fraud losses, faster detection, lower incident response costs, fewer false positives, or the number of AI agents secured? What measurable outcome should customers expect to see before they conclude that agentic security is more than a new cybersecurity category?
Customer success must be assessed not in terms of the number of AI agents that are secured or of newly developed features but on the basis of tangible business results. The best signs of success are the reduction of identity-related attacks, losses from fraud, and unauthorized access attempts and faster threat detection and response. The organization must experience the reduction of MTTD and MTTR, the reduction of false positives, a decrease in operational expenses due to automatic investigation, and compliance due to having the tamper-proof audit trail. With the rise of AI adoption, the other very important metric is the ratio of autonomous actions that are continuously validated and performed within the approved risk limits without affecting the business process.
Reduced privilege exposure due to JIT access and reduced policy violations should also be considered. At the end of the day, customer success must be observed in increased trust in autonomous AI systems where all agent actions are explainable, attributable, and governed by the continuous identity assessment. When an organization can successfully scale up AI agents without increasing security risks and improving operational efficiency and resilience, agentic security proves its business value. investigation,
The larger issue emerging from the discussion is that enterprises cannot treat AI agents simply as another category of software users.
Once an agent can make decisions and take actions across multiple systems, identity becomes closely linked to behavior, context, privilege, and accountability. That makes continuous verification more important than a one-time authentication event.
For banks and other large enterprises, the challenge will be to introduce these controls without slowing down legitimate automated workflows. The success of agentic security will therefore depend not just on detecting malicious activity but also on creating a system where autonomous actions can be allowed at scale while remaining explainable, attributable, and within defined business limits.
As AI agents become more deeply embedded in enterprise operations, securing the identity of the agent may become only the starting point. The harder question will be whether organizations can continuously establish that the agent is doing what it was authorized to do.

ai_security.title: An Agentic Approach for Active Data Collection, Travel Behavior Modeling, and Weather-Sensitive Demand Prediction
ai_security.abstract: Travel behavior research increasingly combines digital data collection with predictive modeling, yet these stages are often developed and evaluated separately. This study proposes a three-agent workflow integrating conversational data collection, structured data processing, and behavioral prediction. A chatbot-administered, image-augmented stated-preference survey collected mode choices from student commuters across five predefined weather scenarios, yielding 454 respondent-scenario observations. Weather-related associations were analyzed using a multinomial logit model, while logistic regression and random forest provided machine-learning benchmarks. Nine locally deployed large language models (LLMs), ranging from 2 to 35 billion parameters, were evaluated across four zero-shot prompt-and-context conditions and extended through persona, few-shot, and vision-based configurations. Random forest achieved 69.6% five-class accuracy, while the best text-only zero-shot LLM reached 69.9% without task-specific fitting. Habitual travel information produced the most consistent gains, Expert framing generally outperformed Role-Play, and persona information was most useful when habitual travel information was unavailable. Few-shot prompting improved prediction for several models, with gains stabilizing after a small number of examples. Using the same weather images shown to respondents, the best vision-based configuration reached 71.5% five-class accuracy, indicating that visual context may provide additional predictive information for selected models. Overall, the study shows how conversational surveys, structured data processing, conventional behavioral modeling, machine learning, and multimodal LLM prediction can be coordinated within an auditable multi-agent workflow.

ai_security.title: PolicyGuide: From Guarding One Action to Guiding the Whole Workflow for Policy-Compliant LLM Agents
ai_security.abstract: Customer-service LLM agents must follow organizational policy when acting on a user's behalf. Compliance failures arise from either forbidden actions, such as granting an ineligible change, or omitted procedural requirements, such as identification or confirmation. Runtime safeguards can intervene on risky actions, but action-local checks do not guide an agent through a multi-step procedure. Workflow-following systems support prescribed process execution, but primarily target workflow completion rather than safeguarding agent behavior. PolicyGuide instead compiles each domain policy into a workflow graph and invokes a proactive verifier at user-turn boundaries. From persisted graph state, the verifier reconciles open requests and returns step-specific remediation along a policy-compliant path. Across the τ^2-bench airline, retail, and telecom domains with a GPT-5.4 agent and verifier, PolicyGuide raises mean Pass^4 from 0.42 to 0.62, with the largest gain on telecom (0.19 to 0.61), the most workflow-structured domain. The same workflows transfer to Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Gemini 2.5 Pro agents. Complementary evaluations find the lowest observed attack-success rate under adversarial users and the strongest procedural compliance in an author-designed workflow-level validation.

ai_security.title: ConceptGuard: Benchmarking Context-Sensitive Unlearning in Large Language Models
ai_security.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly require selective removal of harmful or sensitive knowledge, called unlearning, yet existing methods and benchmarks fail to evaluate this capability completely. Current approaches rely on disjoint forget and retain sets composed of independent facts, and measure success using simple and direct factual recall. This framing fails to capture a key requirement of unlearning, namely the ability to eliminate harmful behaviors while preserving benign and beneficial knowledge. We argue that effective unlearning must operate at the level of concepts, ensuring complete removal of unsafe applications while maintaining their correct and useful usage, thereby achieving conceptually meaningful and complete unlearning. To better evaluate unlearning techniques from such a practical viewpoint, we introduce the notion of dual-use concepts: concepts that can be used in both harmful and benign contexts. Building on these concepts, we construct a benchmark called ConceptGuard where forget and retain sets are explicitly complementary in concept usage. Our benchmark uniquely enables unlearning to be explored and gauged at the level of concepts, instead of sparse facts, and evaluation is intent-sensitive with the goal of maximizing contextual separation to promote safer behavior. We demonstrate that current unlearning techniques perform poorly under this setting, showing weak contextual separation alongside poor performance in ROUGE and concept-level metrics. Our results reveal strong forgetting-utility trade-offs, limited gains in contextual sensitivity, and poor consistency in concept-level control across methods, and provide ideas for unlearning approaches that better align with real-world safety requirements. Our dataset is publicly available.
